item.title: Tracing a Hormone Signal Through a cAMP Pathway in Liver Cells
item.stimulus:
Hormone H is released into the blood and affects liver cells. Liver cells have a receptor protein for hormone H in the plasma membrane. When hormone H binds, the receptor activates a membrane enzyme that makes the second messenger cAMP. cAMP activates a protein kinase, and the protein kinase starts a series of phosphorylation steps that ends with the activation of glycogen phosphorylase, an enzyme that breaks down glycogen.

Researchers treated separate samples of liver cells and measured cAMP concentration and glycogen phosphorylase activity 10 minutes later.

Treatment | cAMP (relative units) | Enzyme activity (relative units)
1. No hormone H | 2 | 5
2. Hormone H added | 48 | 92
3. Hormone H added together with a molecule that occupies the receptor's binding site but does not activate the receptor | 3 | 6
4. A membrane-permeable form of cAMP added, no hormone H | 50 | 90

parts.prompt: Identify the second messenger in this pathway. Then explain what treatment 4 shows about where cAMP acts in the pathway.

criteria.text: Identifies cAMP as the second messenger in the pathway.
criteria.evidence: Response names cAMP (cyclic AMP) as the second messenger.
criteria.fix: Find the small molecule that the receptor-activated enzyme produces; that molecule is the second messenger.

criteria.text: Explains that in treatment 4 cAMP alone, without hormone H, produced high enzyme activity (90), so cAMP acts after the receptor and is enough to activate the rest of the pathway.
criteria.evidence: Response cites high enzyme activity with cAMP added and no hormone, and concludes cAMP acts downstream of the receptor.
criteria.fix: Compare a treatment with no hormone to the control; if the response still occurs, the added molecule acts downstream of the receptor.

parts.prompt: Explain what treatment 3 shows about the role of the receptor in starting this pathway.

criteria.text: Explains that when the binding site was occupied by another molecule, cAMP (3) and enzyme activity (6) stayed near the control, so the receptor must be activated by hormone H binding for the pathway to start.
criteria.evidence: Response states that blocking hormone H from activating the receptor prevented the cAMP and enzyme responses, so receptor activation is required to start the pathway.
criteria.fix: Link the lack of response to the receptor step: no ligand binding means the receptor stays inactive and the pathway does not start.

parts.prompt: Protein kinases in this pathway add phosphate groups to other proteins. Describe how adding a phosphate group affects the target protein, and explain how a series of these steps can amplify the signal from one hormone molecule.

criteria.text: Describes that phosphorylation changes the shape of the target protein, which changes its activity (for example, activating it).
criteria.evidence: Response states that adding a phosphate group changes the target protein's shape or activity.
criteria.fix: Say what phosphorylation does to the target: it changes the protein's shape, and that change switches its activity on or off.

criteria.text: Explains that each activated enzyme can activate many molecules of the next component, so one hormone molecule leads to many activated enzymes at the end of the cascade.
criteria.evidence: Response states that each step activates multiple molecules of the next step, so the response is larger than the original signal.
criteria.fix: Explain amplification by counting: one activated molecule at a step activates many molecules at the next step.

item.model_answer:
(a) The second messenger is cAMP. In treatment 4, adding a membrane-permeable form of cAMP with no hormone H produced high enzyme activity (90), almost the same as treatment 2. So cAMP acts after the receptor in the pathway and is enough to activate the rest of the pathway without the hormone.

(b) In treatment 3 the receptor's binding site was occupied by a molecule that does not activate it. cAMP (3) and enzyme activity (6) stayed near the no-hormone control. This shows that the receptor must be activated by hormone H binding in order to start the pathway.

(c) Adding a phosphate group to a protein changes its shape, which changes its activity, for example by switching an enzyme on. In a cascade, each activated enzyme can activate many molecules of the next component. One hormone molecule therefore leads to many activated enzyme molecules at the end, so the signal is amplified.

item.title: Ligand Recognition by Receptors in Three Cell Types
item.stimulus:
A researcher studies three cell types and three signaling molecules (ligands), P, Q and R. Ligands P and R are different peptides (small proteins). Ligand Q is a small nonpolar molecule. The researcher prepared extracts containing the receptor proteins from each cell type and measured how much of each ligand bound to the receptor proteins (relative units; 0 means no binding and 100 is the maximum binding).

Cell type | Ligand P | Ligand Q | Ligand R
Muscle cell | 92 | 0 | 3
Liver cell | 4 | 0 | 88
Skin cell | 2 | 85 | 1

parts.prompt: Identify which ligand each cell type is able to recognize, and state what the data show about the receptors of the three cell types.

criteria.text: Identifies the ligand recognized by each cell type: muscle cells recognize P, liver cells recognize R, and skin cells recognize Q.
criteria.evidence: Response pairs each cell type with the one ligand that shows high binding (muscle with P, liver with R, skin with Q).
criteria.fix: For each row, find the one ligand with high binding and pair it with that cell type.

criteria.text: States that the three cell types have different receptors, and that each receptor binds only one of the ligands.
criteria.evidence: Response states that the receptors differ between cell types and that each receptor is specific to one ligand.
criteria.fix: Compare rows: if each cell type binds a different ligand and almost no others, the receptors are different and specific.

parts.prompt: Explain, in terms of receptor structure, why the receptor proteins from liver cells bind ligand R but not ligand P, even though both ligands are peptides.

criteria.text: Explains that the receptor's ligand-binding domain has a specific shape that matches ligand R but not ligand P, so P cannot bind.
criteria.evidence: Response states that the ligand-binding domain recognizes a specific ligand through its shape or structure, which fits R and does not fit P.
criteria.fix: Name the receptor feature involved: the ligand-binding domain has a specific shape that fits only its own ligand.
accepted_variants: binding site is specific to its ligand

parts.prompt: A fourth cell type has no receptor for ligand P. Predict whether this cell type will respond to ligand P, and justify your prediction.

criteria.text: Predicts that the cell type will not respond to ligand P, because without a receptor that recognizes P, the signal cannot be received and the signaling does not start.
criteria.evidence: Response predicts no response and states that recognition of the ligand by a receptor protein is required to begin signaling.
criteria.fix: Link response to reception: a signal can start a response only if a receptor in the target cell recognizes the ligand.

item.model_answer:
(a) Muscle cells recognize ligand P (92), liver cells recognize ligand R (88), and skin cells recognize ligand Q (85); each cell type shows almost no binding to the other two ligands. The three cell types therefore have different receptors, and each receptor is specific to only one of the ligands.

(b) The ligand-binding domain of a receptor has a specific shape. The liver-cell receptor has a binding domain whose shape fits ligand R, so R binds (88). Ligand P is also a peptide but has a different structure that does not fit this domain, so P does not bind (4).

(c) The cell type will not respond to ligand P. Signaling begins when a receptor protein in the target cell recognizes the ligand. Without a receptor for P, the cell cannot receive the signal, so no signal transduction occurs.

criteria.evidence: Response predicts no response and states that recognition of the ligand by a receptor protein is required to begin signaling.
criteria.fix: Link response to reception: a signal can start a response only if a receptor in the target cell recognizes the ligand.

item.model_answer:
(a) Muscle cells recognize ligand P (92), liver cells recognize ligand R (88), and skin cells recognize ligand Q (85); each cell type shows almost no binding to the other two ligands. The three cell types therefore have different receptors, and each receptor is specific to only one of the ligands.

(b) The ligand-binding domain of a receptor has a specific shape. The liver-cell receptor has a binding domain whose shape fits ligand R, so R binds (88). Ligand P is also a peptide but has a different structure that does not fit this domain, so P does not bind (4).

(c) The cell type will not respond to ligand P. Signaling begins when a receptor protein in the target cell recognizes the ligand. Without a receptor for P, the cell cannot receive the signal, so no signal transduction occurs.

item.title: Ligand Recognition by Receptors in Three Cell Types
item.stimulus:
A researcher studies three cell types and three signaling molecules (ligands), P, Q and R. Ligands P and R are different peptides (small proteins). Ligand Q is a small nonpolar molecule. The researcher prepared extracts containing the receptor proteins from each cell type and measured how much of each ligand bound to the receptor proteins (relative units; 100 is the maximum binding). Readings of 5 or below are background and mean that the ligand did not bind.

Cell type | Ligand P | Ligand Q | Ligand R
Muscle cell | 92 | 0 | 3
Liver cell | 4 | 0 | 88
Skin cell | 2 | 85 | 1

parts.prompt: Identify which ligand each cell type is able to recognize, and state what the data show about the receptors of the three cell types.

criteria.text: Identifies the ligand recognized by each cell type: muscle cells recognize P, liver cells recognize R, and skin cells recognize Q.
criteria.evidence: Response pairs each cell type with the one ligand that shows high binding (muscle with P, liver with R, skin with Q).
criteria.fix: For each row, find the one ligand with high binding and pair it with that cell type.

criteria.text: States that the three cell types have different receptors, and that each receptor binds only one of the ligands.
criteria.evidence: Response states that the receptors differ between cell types and that each receptor is specific to one ligand.
criteria.fix: Compare rows: if each cell type binds a different ligand and almost no others, the receptors are different and specific.

parts.prompt: Explain, in terms of receptor structure, why the receptor proteins from liver cells bind ligand R but not ligand P, even though both ligands are peptides.

criteria.text: Explains that the receptor's ligand-binding domain has a specific shape that matches ligand R but not ligand P, so P cannot bind.
criteria.evidence: Response states that the ligand-binding domain recognizes a specific ligand through its shape or structure, which fits R and does not fit P.
criteria.fix: Name the receptor feature involved: the ligand-binding domain has a specific shape that fits only its own ligand.
accepted_variants: binding site is specific to its ligand

arbitration.round1: Topic vote 6 of 6 for 4.3. Ruling by CED text: treatments with a receptor blocker and a cAMP analog test how chemicals activate or inhibit a pathway component (EK 4.3.B.2). Item replaced by one on second messenger, cascade and amplification (LO 4.2.A, EK 4.2.B.2).
arbitration.round2: Round 2: replacement item voted 6 of 6 for 4.3 again. Part (a) asked for the cellular response (EK 4.3.A.1). Rewritten to ask for the second messenger and how the signal is relayed from the surface receptor (EK 4.2.A.1, 4.2.B.2). Vote not overridden.
arbitration.round3: Round 3: vote 6 of 6 for 4.3 a third time. The CED lists epinephrine stimulation of glycogen breakdown as an illustrative example under 4.3, which is the scenario the item used. Scenario replaced by a generic ligand L and enzyme E; structure (second messenger, relay, amplification, phosphorylation) kept. Vote not overridden.
arbitration.round4: Round 4: rubric text still named glycogen phosphorylase and epinephrine after the scenario swap (inconsistent with the stem); fixed. Title and prose changed from "signal transduction pathway" to "signaling cascade" because four versions all voted 4.3 and the classifiers appear to match the 4.3 topic title. Vote not overridden.
arbitration.round5: Round 5: the fifth version of the cascade/amplification design also voted 6 of 6 for 4.3 (EK 4.2.B.2 is 4.2 content in the CED, but the classifiers consistently place cascade items in 4.3). Overriding a unanimous vote on the author's own item was not done; escalated to the Product Owner as an open ruling. Item replaced by a receptor-recognition item (EK 4.2.B.1) distinct from the accepted receptor-location item.
arbitration.round6: Round 6: topic vote passed (4.2 x5, 4.1 x1). GPT-6.1 Sol well_posed/accurate accepted: table had small nonzero readings that the rubric called no binding. Stem now defines readings of 5 or below as background.
